translations.text: God's church celebrates this day in honour of the great apostle Paul, because he is called the teacher of all nations:
through true teaching. His martyrdom, however, was accomplished together with the blessed Peter.
He was brought up from childhood in the old law, and was steeped in it with great zeal.
After Christ's passion, when the true faith sprang up through the preaching of the apostles, he persecuted Christian people through his ignorance,
and put them in prison, and he also consented to the killing of the first martyr, Stephen. Yet it is not read of him that he killed anyone with his own hands.
"He then took letters from the chief priests to the city of Damascus, so that he might bind the Christians whom he found in that city and lead them to Jerusalem.
Then it happened on that journey that a great light suddenly came upon him and threw him to the ground, and he heard a voice from above saying, 'Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
It will be bad for you yourself to kick against the goad.' Then with great fear he answered the voice, 'Who are you, dear Lord?'
The call of the divine voice answered him, 'I am the Saviour whom you persecute. But rise now and go on to the city; there you will be told what it is fitting for you to do.'
Then he arose with blinded eyes, and his companions led him, blind as he was, to the city. And waiting there, he tasted neither food nor drink for the space of three days."
"There was a servant of God in that city whose name was Ananias. The Lord spoke to him in these words: 'Ananias, arise and go to my servant Saul, who is praying for my mercy with an earnest mind.'
He answered the Lord's voice, 'My Saviour, how can I speak to him, who is a persecutor of your saints by the authority of the chief priests?'
The Lord said, 'Go as I have told you, for he is a chosen vessel to me, to carry my name to nations, and kings, and the children of Israel; and he shall suffer much for my name.'
Then Ananias came to the chosen champion and laid his hands on him with this greeting: "Saul, my brother, the Saviour, who spoke to you on the way, has sent me to you,
that you may see, and be filled with the Holy Spirit.' Then, at these words, something like membranes fell from his eyes, and he immediately received his sight, and turned to baptism.
He then remained a few days with God's servants in the city, and with great boldness preached to the Jews that Christ, whom they had rejected, is the Son of Almighty God.
They were greatly astonished and said, "Why, is this not the cruel persecutor of Christian men? How is it that he preaches the faith of Christ?"
Saul truly grew much stronger, and confounded the Jews, steadfastly affirming that Christ is the Son of God."
"Then, after many days, the Jews plotted how they might kill God's champion, and set guards at every gate of the city.
Paul perceived their plot, and the Christians took him and let him down over the wall in a basket.
And he went back to Jerusalem and made himself known to the holy company of Christ's household, and told them how the Saviour had spoken to him from heaven.
Afterwards, after some time, a call came from the Holy Spirit to the faithful company, saying, "Send Paul and Barnabas to the work for which I have chosen them."
Then the holy company, at God's command and by his choice, sent them out to teach all peoples about Christ's coming for the redemption of the world."
"Barnabas was then Paul's companion in the preaching for a long time. Then at last they thought it best to go their separate ways, and so they did.
Paul was then filled and comforted with the gift of the Holy Spirit, and went to many peoples, sowing God's seed.
In one city he stayed twelve months, in another two years, in another three, and he appointed bishops, priests and servants of God. Then he travelled on to another people and did the same.
Afterwards he sent letters back to the believers he had taught before, and with those letters he urged them on and strengthened them in the way of life."
We will now go through this reading with a short explanation and make it clear, in case it holds anything hidden. Paul persecuted Christians, not out of malice,
as the Jews did. Rather, he was a spokesman and defender of the old law, with great steadfastness: he thought that the faith of Christ was opposed to the old ordinance.
But the Saviour, who established the old law with various figures, was the same who later, when he was present, turned them into truth according to their spiritual meaning.
Paul did not then understand the spiritual meaning of the law, and so he was its advocate and a persecutor of faith in Christ.
God Almighty, who knows all things, saw his intention: that he did not persecute faithful men out of malice,
but because he was guarding the old law. And then He spoke to him from heaven, saying, "Saul, why are you persecuting me?
I am the Truth that you are defending yourself against. Stop this persecution: it is harmful for you to kick against the goad.
If the ox kicks against the goad, it hurts itself. In the same way, your struggle against me harms you." He said, "Why are you persecuting me?"

because he is the head of Christian men, and he grieves over whatever his limbs suffer on earth, as he said through his prophet: "Whoever touches you, it will be as painful to me as if he touched the pupil of my eye."
He was thrown to the ground and said, "Who are you, Lord?" His pride was thrown down, and true humility was raised up in him.
He fell unrighteous and was raised up righteous. As he fell he lost his bodily sight. As he rose he received the enlightenment of his mind.
He remained without sight for three days, because he had denied Christ's resurrection on the third day.
In the Hebrew language, Ananias means 'sheep.' That gentle sheep then baptized the wicked Saul and made him the devout Paul.
He baptised the wolf and made him into a lamb. He changed his name along with his ways, and he who had earlier afflicted God's church with fierce persecution was then its true herald.
He wanted to escape the plotting of the Jewish people, and he allowed himself to be let down over the wall in a basket. This was not because he was unwilling to suffer death for faith in Christ,
but he escaped an untimely death because he first had to win many people for God through his great wisdom, and only afterwards, with great honour, stretch out his neck for martyrdom.
Afterwards he suffered far greater torments for Christ's name than he had inflicted on Christians before his conversion.
Saul the wicked scourged the Christians, but after his conversion the devout Paul was often scourged for Christ's name.
Once he was stoned almost to death, so that the persecutors left him for dead. But the next morning he got up and went on with his preaching.
He was often in great danger, both at sea and on land, in the wilderness, among robbers, in hunger and in thirst, and in many vigils, in cold and in nakedness, and in many prisons.
He hurried on with his preaching as if he wanted to bring all mankind to God's kingdom: with teaching, with prayers and with letters, he always urged people toward God's will.
He was taken up to heaven as far as the third level, and there he saw and heard secrets of God that he was not allowed to reveal to anyone.
He mourned other people's sins with weeping, and he showed a father's love to all the faithful.
By the work of his hands he provided for the [?] of himself and his companions. Besides this, nothing is known in true religion that his teaching did not establish.
By God's command, the other apostles lived from their teaching, and they did so without blame.
Paul alone, however, who was a tentmaker by trade, would not accept the support he was allowed. He provided for his own needs and those of his companions with his own labour.
His teachings and his way of life are beyond our understanding, but blessed is he who diligently obeys his exhortations.
Simon Peter said to Jesus: and so on.
"He left all worldly things and followed the Saviour alone," as the gospel you have just heard at this service says.
"At that time Peter the apostle said to the Saviour, 'See, we have left all worldly things and follow you alone. What will you give us as a reward for this?'" and so on.
Great confidence stirred in Peter's heart: he alone spoke for the whole company, "We have left all things." What did Peter leave?
He was a fisherman, and made his living by that trade, and yet he said with great boldness, "We have left all things."
But he left much, and so did his brothers, when they gave up the desire to own. Even if someone leaves great possessions, if he does not leave covetousness, he has not left all things.
Peter left behind little things, a bag and a net, but he left behind all things when, for the love of God, he would have nothing.
He said, "We follow you." It is not perfect to give up many possessions unless one follows God.
Truly, the heathen philosophers left many things, as Socrates did, who exchanged all his possessions for a single wedge of gold,
and afterwards threw the wedge into the wide sea, so that covetousness for possessions would not hinder his will and draw him away from the worldly learning that he loved:

but doing so did not profit him, because he did not follow God but his own will, and therefore he did not have the heavenly reward with the apostles, who despised all worldly things for the love of Christ and followed him in obedience.
Then Peter asked, "What shall happen to us? We have done as you commanded us; what will you give us as a reward?"
The Saviour answered, "Truly I tell you, you who follow me shall sit on twelve judgment seats in the regeneration, when I sit on the throne of my majesty;
and then you will judge the twelve tribes of Israel." By "regeneration" he meant the general resurrection, in which our bodies will be regenerated to incorruption, that is, to eternal things.
We are born twice in this life: the first birth is fleshly, from father and from mother;
the second birth is spiritual, when we are born again in holy baptism, in which all sins are forgiven us through the grace of the Holy Spirit.
The third birth will be at the general resurrection, in which our bodies will be born again as incorruptible bodies.
At the resurrection the twelve apostles will sit with Christ on their judgment seats and judge the twelve tribes of the people of Israel. This twelvefold number has great significance.
If only the twelve tribes are judged at the great judgment, what then becomes of the thirteenth tribe, Levi?
What becomes of all the nations of the world? Do you think that they will be set apart from the judgment?
But this twelvefold number is set for all mankind throughout the whole world, because of the perfection of its significance.
There are twelve hours in the day, and twelve months in the year; there are twelve patriarchs, twelve prophets, twelve apostles;
and this number has a greater meaning than the unlearned can understand. So this twelvefold number signifies the whole circle of the world.
The apostles and all the chosen who followed their example will be judges with Christ on the great day.
There will be four companies at the judgment, two of chosen people and two of the rejected.
The first company is that of the apostles and those who follow their example, who gave up all worldly things for God's name. They will be the judges, and no judgment will be passed on them.
The second order is that of faithful laypeople. Judgment is appointed for them, such that they will be separated from the fellowship of the rejected,
as the Lord says: "Come to me, you blessed of my Father, and receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you from the beginning of the world."
One order is that of the rejected who had knowledge of God, but did not practise their faith by keeping God's commandments. These will be condemned.
The other order is that of the heathens, who had no knowledge of God. In them the apostle's saying is fulfilled: "Those who sinned without God's law will also perish without any law."
To these two orders the righteous Judge will then say, "Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the devil and his accursed spirits."
The gospel says further, "Everyone who leaves, for my name's sake, father or mother, brothers or sisters,
wife or children, land or buildings, will be repaid a hundredfold, and in addition he will have eternal life."
The number one hundred is perfect, and he who leaves perishable things for God's name will receive the spiritual reward a hundredfold from God.
This saying applies especially to people in the monastic order, who for the joy of the kingdom of heaven leave father and mother and fleshly kin.

They receive many spiritual fathers and spiritual brothers, because all the people of that order who live according to the rule are counted as fathers and brothers to them, and in addition they are enriched with the reward of eternal life.
Those who despise all worldly things at God's command, and have their sustenance from common property, are perfect and are ranked with the apostles.
The others, who do not have this dignity, that they are able to leave all their possessions together,
Let them then give, for God's name, the portion that they can afford, and whatever they give singly for a time will be repaid to them a hundredfold forever.
There is a great difference among those who have turned to the religious life: some of them imitate the apostles, some imitate Judas, Christ's betrayer, some Ananias and Sapphira, and some Gehazi.
Those who, in imitation of the apostles, despise all transitory things for the sake of eternal life will have praise and the eternal reward with Christ's apostles.
Whoever lives among monks and deceitfully cheats the monastery of its possessions is the companion of Judas, who betrayed Christ, and he will receive his punishment with the inhabitants of hell.
He who turns to the monastic life with a double mind, giving away part of his possessions and keeping part for himself, and who has no trust in the Almighty

to provide him with food and clothing and his other needs, receives the accursed sentence along with Ananias and Sapphira, who cheated over their own possessions and fell down dead by a sudden death before the apostles.
He who is discontented in the monastic life, and longs for the things that he did not have in the life of the world, or could not get,
without doubt resembles the leper Gehazi, the prophet's servant; and what Gehazi suffered in his body, this man suffers in his soul.
This servant followed the great prophet Elisha. A powerful man came to him from the land called Syria. His name was Naaman, and he was a leper.
He came to Elisha, the prophet of God, in the land of Judea, and Elisha healed him of the disease by God's power.
Then Naaman offered the man of God precious treasures for his healing. The prophet answered him, "God's power healed you, not I. I will not accept your money:
thank God for your health, and enjoy your possessions." Naaman then returned with all his company to his own people.

Then the prophet's servant Gehazi was overcome by greed. He ran off after the nobleman Naaman and deceived him with these words: "Two sons of the prophets have just now suddenly come to my master: send him two garments and a pound."
The nobleman answered him, "It would be mean to send him so little; take four garments and two pounds." Gehazi then went back with the treasures and hid his errand from the prophet.
The prophet asked him, "Where have you come from, Gehazi?" He answered, "Sir, I have not been anywhere."
The prophet said: "I saw, through God's Spirit, when the nobleman got down from his chariot and went to meet you, and you took his payments in money and in clothing.
[?] "Now along with the treasures you shall also have his leprosy from now on, you and all your offspring forever." And Gehazi left his presence, struck with leprosy as white as snow.
Therefore people in the monastic order must avoid these evil examples with great care, and imitate the apostles, so that they may have eternal life with them and with God. Amen.
